thesis: Whether the mind is nothing but a bundle of perceptions with no real connexion among them that can ground personal identity (Hume first asserts the bundle view, then confesses he cannot render his own principles consistent).

early.text: But setting aside some metaphysicians of this kind, I may venture to affirm of the rest of mankind, that they are nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed each other with an inconceivable rapidity, and are in a perpetual flux and movement.
early.work: A Treatise of Human Nature, Book I, Part IV, Sect. VI "Of Personal Identity"
early.locator: Book I, Part IV, Section VI

announced.text: I had entertained some hopes, that however deficient our theory of the intellectual world might be, it would be free from those contradictions, and absurdities, which seem to attend every explication, that human reason can give of the material world. But upon a more strict review of the section concerning personal identity, I find myself involved in such a labyrinth, that, I must confess, I neither know how to correct my former opinions, nor how to render them consistent.
announced.work: A Treatise of Human Nature, Appendix

control.text: We speak not strictly and philosophically when we talk of the combat of passion and of reason. Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions, and can never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.
control.work: A Treatise of Human Nature, Book II, Part III, Sect. III
control.locator: Book II, Part III, Section III "Of the influencing motives of the will"

notes: Gutenberg #4705 is the combined Treatise text; Book I/II appeared 1739, Book III and the Appendix 1740. No translator (English original). The control concerns reason and the passions, a separate thesis that Hume does not retract in the Appendix.

thesis: Whether an untested diamond that is never scratched is hard only as a matter of usage (1878 pragmatic maxim, nominalist-leaning) or has a real, though never actualised, hardness (1905 realism about real possibilities).

early.text: There is absolutely no difference between a hard thing and a soft thing so long as they are not brought to the test. Suppose, then, that a diamond could be crystallized in the midst of a cushion of soft cotton, and should remain there until it was finally burned up. Would it be false to say that that diamond was soft?
early.work: "Illustrations of the Logic of Science II: How to Make Our Ideas Clear", Popular Science Monthly 12
early.locator: Section III (Popular Science Monthly 12, Jan 1878, about p. 301)

announced.text: The question is, was that diamond really hard? It is certain that no discernible actual fact determined it to be so. But is its hardness not, nevertheless, a real fact? To say, as the article of Jan. 1878 seems to intend, that it is just as an arbitrary “usage of speech” chooses to arrange its thoughts, is as much as to decide against the reality of the property, since the real is that which is such as it is regardless of how it is, at any time, thought to be.
announced.locator: The Monist 15(4), Oct 1905, pp. 481-499; passage lies between printed pages 493 and 496 (exact page not pinned down)

control.text: Consider what effects, which might conceivably have practical bearings, we conceive the object of our conception to have. Then, our conception of these effects is the whole of our conception of the object.
control.work: "How to Make Our Ideas Clear", Popular Science Monthly 12
control.locator: Section II, end (statement of the third grade of clearness)

notes: The announced passage does not say "I was wrong" in the first person; it says the 1878 article "seems to intend" a view that decides against the reality of the property, and in a nearby sentence (not used here because the OCR is garbled) says the writer "wavered in his own mind" and calls the word MERELY an "abominable falsehood". The 1905 source is an archive.org OCR of the Monist issue (curly quotes, no hyphenation inside the passage). The 1878 source is a Wikisource render of the Popular Science Monthly page; the saved file contains stray JSON template debris elsewhere but not inside the passages. The control (the pragmatic maxim) is retained by Peirce in 1905. IEP page opened and states Peirce returned to the issue "with some regret".

thesis: Whether tragic art gives a metaphysical comfort and expresses Schopenhauerian metaphysics (The Birth of Tragedy, 1872) or whether that was a mistake to be laughed away (1886 'Attempt at a Self-Criticism').

early.text: The metaphysical comfort,--with which, as I have here intimated, every true tragedy dismisses us--that, in spite of the perpetual change of phenomena, life at bottom is indestructibly powerful and pleasurable, this comfort appears with corporeal lucidity as the satyric chorus, as the chorus of natural beings, who live ineradicable as it were behind all civilisation, and who, in spite of the ceaseless change of generations and the history of nations, remain for ever the same.
early.locator: The Birth of Tragedy, section 7 (original 1872; translation 1909)

announced.text: How I now regret, that I had not then the courage (or immodesty?) to allow myself, in all respects, the use of an _individual language_ for such _individual_ contemplations and ventures in the field of thought--that I laboured to express, in Kantian and Schopenhauerian formulæ, strange and new valuations, which ran fundamentally counter to the spirit of Kant and Schopenhauer, as well as to their taste!
announced.work: The Birth of Tragedy, "An Attempt at Self-Criticism" (1886 preface), section 6

unannounced.text: No! ye should first of all learn the art of earthly comfort, ye should learn to _laugh,_ my young friends, if ye are at all determined to remain pessimists: if so, you will perhaps, as laughing ones, eventually send all metaphysical comfortism to the devil--and metaphysics first of all!
unannounced.work: The Birth of Tragedy, "An Attempt at Self-Criticism" (1886 preface), section 7

control.text: We shall have gained much for the science of æsthetics, when once we have perceived not only by logical inference, but by the immediate certainty of intuition, that the continuous development of art is bound up with the duplexity of the _Apollonian_ and the _Dionysian:_ in like manner as procreation is dependent on the duality of the sexes, involving perpetual conflicts with only periodically intervening reconciliations.

notes: The unannounced item is from the same 1886 preface as the announced one, so it is not a separate later text; it states the later view in the second person ("ye") with no "I was wrong". Drop it if a separate-text unannounced item is required. The SEP aesthetics entry documents that Nietzsche's later aesthetics is set up in opposition to Schopenhauer and that whether The Birth accepts Schopenhauer's metaphysics is disputed; it does not quote the Self-Criticism. The control (Apollonian/Dionysian duplexity) is a claim Nietzsche keeps. Gutenberg marks italics with underscores (_word_); they are left in the announced, unannounced and control passages exactly as in the file.

thesis: Whether Wagner is the sublime protagonist of the revival of art as the highest metaphysical activity (1871 dedication) or a sickness and symptom of decadence he once took too seriously (1888).

early.text: These earnest ones may be informed that I am convinced that art is the highest task and the properly metaphysical activity of this life, as it is understood by the man, to whom, as my sublime protagonist on this path, I would now dedicate this essay.
early.work: The Birth of Tragedy, "Foreword to Richard Wagner"
early.locator: Foreword to Richard Wagner (dated Basel, end of 1871; translation 1909)

announced.text: And yet I was one of the most corrupted Wagnerites.… I was able to take Wagner seriously. Oh, this old magician! what tricks has he not played upon us! The first thing his art places in our hands is a magnifying glass: we look through it, and we no longer trust our own eyes
announced.locator: The Case of Wagner (Turin, May 1888), section 3 (3rd edition, Foulis 1911)

unannounced.text: I place this point of view first and foremost: Wagner’s art is diseased. The problems he sets on the stage are all concerned with hysteria; the convulsiveness of his emotions, his over-excited sensitiveness, his taste which demands ever sharper condimentation, his erraticness which he togged out to look like principles, and, last but not least, his choice of heroes and heroines, considered as physiological types (—a hospital ward!—): the whole represents a morbid picture; of this there can be no doubt.

control.text: In order to assign also to Socrates the dignity of such a leading position, it will suffice to recognise in him the type of an unheard-of form of existence, the type of the _theoretical man,_ with regard to whose meaning and purpose it will be our next task to attain an insight.
control.locator: The Birth of Tragedy, section 15 (Socrates as the theoretical man)

notes: The unannounced passage is from the same work as the announced passage (a later section), so it is a later-text statement of the later view without a "changed my mind" line, but not from a different book. The announced passage is an admission about the author's past stance ("I was one of the most corrupted Wagnerites ... I was able to take Wagner seriously"), not a point-by-point retraction. SEP aesthetics entry documents the later anti-Schopenhauerian turn but not Wagner specifically; no better secondary was opened. The control passage keeps the Gutenberg italic underscore markup (_theoretical man).

thesis: Whether the understanding can know things as they are (Inaugural Dissertation 1770, intellectual presentations represent things as they are) or only objects of possible experience and mere appearances (Prolegomena 1783).

early.text: it is plain that what is sensuously thought is the representation of things as they appear, while the intellectual presentations are the representations of things as they are.
early.work: Kant's Inaugural Dissertation of 1770 (On the Form and Principles of the Sensible and Intelligible World), Section II
early.locator: Section II "Distinction of the sensuous from the intellectual in general", Paragraph 4 (original 1770; Eckoff translation 1894, Columbia College)

announced.text: I openly confess, the suggestion of David Hume was the very thing, which many years ago first interrupted my dogmatic slumber, and gave my investigations in the field of speculative philosophy quite a new direction.
announced.work: Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics, Preface

unannounced.text: Hence if the pure concepts of the understanding do not refer to objects of experience but to things in themselves (noumena), they have no signification whatever. They serve, as it were, only to decipher appearances, that we may be able to read them as experience. The principles which arise from their reference to the sensible world, only serve our understanding for empirical use.
unannounced.work: Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics, section 30

control.text: Space is not something objective and real, neither sub- stance, nor accident, nor relation ; but subjective and ideal, arising by fixed law from the nature of the mind
control.work: Kant's Inaugural Dissertation of 1770, Section III, 'Of Space'
control.locator: Section III, 'Of Space', item D (OCR heading reads 'Paragraph 13'; unverified against standard section numbering)

notes: The early passage is a mid-sentence fragment because an OCR page header interrupts the sentence; it starts at "it is plain that". The Dissertation source is an archive.org OCR (Cornell copy of the 1894 Eckoff translation) with OCR artefacts in the control ("sub- stance" hyphenation and " ;" spacing). The announced passage states a change of direction after Hume but is not an explicit "I held X, I now hold Y"; it announces the break with dogmatism generally. The unannounced item is from the same work as the announced one. SEP page (Kant-Hume) quotes the dogmatic-slumber sentence and discusses which years Kant refers to; it does not itself discuss the 1770 Dissertation claim.

thesis: Whether wages can be affected by anything but the ratio of circulating capital to labourers, so trade combinations cannot raise wages (Principles of Political Economy), which Mill in 1869 declares "deprived of its scientific foundation".

early.text: With these limitations of the terms, wages not only depend upon the relative amount of capital and population, but can not, under the rule of competition, be affected by anything else. Wages (meaning, of course, the general rate) can not rise, but by an increase of the aggregate funds employed in hiring laborers, or a diminution in the number of the competitors for hire; nor fall, except either by a diminution of the funds devoted to paying labor, or by an increase in the number of laborers to be paid.
early.work: Principles of Political Economy (abridged ed. with notes by J. Laurence Laughlin), Book II, Chapter II "Of Wages" (Mill's original Book II, ch. XI)
early.locator: Book II, Chapter II "Of Wages", section 1 in the Laughlin abridgement (Mill's original 1848 Book II ch. XI)

announced.text: The doctrine hitherto taught by all or most economists (including myself), which denied it to be possible that trade combinations can raise wages, or which limited their operation in that respect to the somewhat earlier attainment of a rise which the competition of the market would have produced without them,—this doctrine is deprived of its scientific foundation, and must be thrown aside.
announced.work: "Thornton on Labour and Its Claims", Part I, The Fortnightly Review, new series vol. V, no. XXIX, 1 May 1869
announced.locator: Part I, near the end (about p. 517)

control.text: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
control.work: Principles of Political Economy (Laughlin abridgement), Book II, Chapter I "Of Property", section 1

notes: Early source is the Laughlin 1884 abridgement (Gutenberg #30107) of Mill's 1848 Principles, not the 1848/1865 text itself; the quoted sentences are Mill's but the abridgement may omit surrounding text. The announced passage is explicit ("including myself"). The wages-fund doctrine and trade-union effectiveness are linked: Mill's 1869 passage says the doctrine that combinations cannot raise wages "must be thrown aside", which conflicts with the early claim that wages "can not ... be affected by anything else" under competition. Vint (JSHET 2017) calls it a "double recantation".

thesis: Whether mental phenomena are essentially a relation of acquaintance/consciousness between a subject and an object (Problems of Philosophy 1912) or whether that theory is to be refuted (Analysis of Mind 1921, moving to neutral monism).

early.text: When I am acquainted with 'my seeing the sun', it seems plain that I am acquainted with two different things in relation to each other. On the one hand there is the sense-datum which represents the sun to me, on the other hand there is that which sees this sense-datum. All acquaintance, such as my acquaintance with the sense-datum which represents the sun, seems obviously a relation between the person acquainted and the object with which the person is acquainted.
early.work: The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter V "Knowledge by Acquaintance and Knowledge by Description"

announced.text: In this first lecture I shall be concerned to refute a theory which is widely held, and which I formerly held myself: the theory that the essence of everything mental is a certain quite peculiar something called "consciousness," conceived either as a relation to objects, or as a pervading quality of psychical phenomena.
announced.work: The Analysis of Mind, Lecture I, Recent Criticisms of Consciousness"

unannounced.text: The stuff of which the world of our experience is composed is, in my belief, neither mind nor matter, but something more primitive than either. Both mind and matter seem to be composite, and the stuff of which they are compounded lies in a sense between the two, in a sense above them both, like a common ancestor.
unannounced.work: The Analysis of Mind, Lecture I

control.text: The value of philosophy is, in fact, to be sought largely in its very uncertainty. The man who has no tincture of philosophy goes through life imprisoned in the prejudices derived from common sense, from the habitual beliefs of his age or his nation, and from convictions which have grown up in his mind without the co-operation or consent of his deliberate reason.
control.work: The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter XV "The Value of Philosophy"

notes: The announced passage is a good explicit retraction ("which I formerly held myself"). Lecture I of The Analysis of Mind also says "Until very lately I believed ... Now I no longer believe this" about the object-reference of mental phenomena. The unannounced item is from the same lecture as the announced one. The early passage treats acquaintance as a relation between a subject and an object, i.e. the "relation to objects" view named in the announced passage; Russell in 1912 hedges about acquaintance with the bare self, so the conflict is with the general theory rather than a single sentence. SEP Russell entry says in 1919 he "changed his position and accepted neutral-monism".

thesis: Whether a proposition is a picture of a fact (Tractatus) or its meaning is its use in a language-game (Philosophical Investigations, not public domain).

early.text: 2.1 We make to ourselves pictures of facts. 2.11 The picture presents the facts in logical space, the existence and non - existence of atomic facts. 2.12 The picture is a model of reality.

notes: Later text (Philosophical Investigations, 1953) is not public domain and was not fetched or copied. Source is an archive.org OCR of the 1922 Routledge & Kegan Paul bilingual edition; the passage contains the OCR spacing artefact "non - existence". The SEP entry says the later Wittgenstein critiqued traditional philosophy including his own early work. No control recorded.
